bib.title: Knowledge-Grounded Dialogue Generation with Pre-trained Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Knowledge-Grounded Dialogue Generation with Pre-trained Language Models" (the model is called KnowledGPT), by Xueliang Zhao, Wei Wu, Can Xu, Chongyang Tao, Dongyan Zhao and Rui Yan. EMNLP 2020, pp. 3377–3390. The PDF does not print an arXiv id for this paper. The only arXiv ids in it belong to cited works, and the PDF metadata has none either. I did not supply one from memory.

COVERAGE: I read all 57,269 of 57,269 chars, across 14 pages (printed pp. 3377–3390). That includes the appendices A–E and the case tables 11–12. I skimmed the references (pp. 9–12) for the works the paper builds on. Page numbers below are PDF pages; printed page = 3376 + PDF page.

CLAIMS
- claim: The retrieved knowledge is far larger than GPT-2's input limit, which is why selection is needed.
  number: 61.2 sentences / 1625.6 tokens vs 1024 max
  setup: Wizard of Wikipedia, average per conversation context
  quote: "the maximum number for GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) is 1024), ... on average each conversation context is associated with 61.2 sentences retrieved from wiki articles, and the average number of tokens in the extra knowledge is 1625.6"
  where: p.2

- claim: How it works. A BERT encoder scores each knowledge sentence jointly with the dialogue context (cross-encoder style: [CLS] context [SEP] sentence [SEP]). An LSTM+attention selector then picks sentences one at a time and stops when it picks a special end embedding or reaches Tmax. Only context + the selected sentences go to GPT-2.
  number: Tmax 1 (Wizard), 2 (CMU_DoG); BERT 110M, GPT-2 117M
  setup: implementation details
  quote: "Tmax for D′ is set as 1 in Wizard, and 2 in CMU DoG. We choose BERT (110M) and GPT-2 (117M)"
  where: p.5 (method), p.7 (details)

- claim: Training needs no knowledge labels. (1) A warm-up builds pseudo-labels: sort sentences by unigram F1 to the human response, then keep the prefix that maximises F1. (2) The selector is then trained with REINFORCE, rewarded by the F1 of GPT-2's generated response, minus a mean baseline. (3) GPT-2 is fine-tuned on a curriculum that moves from pseudo-labels to the selector's own picks (Bernoulli p, starting at 1.0 and annealing).
  number: warm-up 1000 steps, batch 64; p anneal rate 1e-5
  setup: both datasets
  quote: "In warming up, we define Sim(·,·) as unigram F1, and optimize g(U,D) and the GPT-2 model with the pseudo ground-truth for 1000 steps with a batch size of 64."
  where: p.5–7

- claim: Main result on Wizard. KnowledGPT gets the best F1 on seen and unseen topics. Its F1 gain is largest on unseen topics.
  number: F1 22.0 seen / 20.5 unseen. The comparisons are DRD 19.3/17.9, SKT* (uses human labels) 19.3/16.1, SKT+GPT-2* 20.3/17.8, GPT-2trunc 18.7/18.3, TMN 15.9/14.3
  setup: Wizard Test Seen/Unseen, unigram F1 against the human response, greedy decoding. Bold entries mark t-test p<0.01
  quote: "KnowledGPT 19.2 22.0 0.872 0.463 0.682 22.3 20.5 0.870 0.452 0.674" (PPL, F1, Average, Extrema, Greedy, seen then unseen)
  where: p.7, Table 2

- claim: Main result on CMU_DoG.
  number: F1 13.5 vs 10.8 for both DRD and GPT-2trunc
  setup: CMU_DoG test set, movie domain
  quote: "KnowledGPT 20.6 13.5 0.837 0.437 0.654"; "GPT-2trunc 18.6 10.8 0.730 0.419 0.597"
  where: p.7, Table 3

- claim: Plain truncation loses the gold knowledge in most cases.
  number: 53%
  setup: GPT-2trunc, Wizard Test Seen+Unseen, gold sentence randomly mixed into the candidates
  quote: "we find that in 53% test examples (Test Seen+Test Unseen), the ground-truth knowledge is cut"
  where: p.7

- claim: Irrelevant knowledge hurts even when nothing is cut. On CMU_DoG all the knowledge fits, yet truncation-free concatenation still loses to selection.
  number: max knowledge length 502 tokens
  setup: CMU_DoG
  quote: "GPT-2 trunc is worse than KnowledGPT on CMU DoG even though we do not cut anything on the knowledge (the maximum length of the knowledge input is 502, and thus is within the constraint of GPT-2)"
  where: p.8

- claim: More knowledge means more noise. With the gold sentence forced into the input, F1 falls steadily as the token budget grows and the gold share shrinks. This is the clearest "less but better context" evidence in the paper.
  number: F1 seen 30.9 (128 tokens) → 25.6 (256) → 21.8 (512) → 20.6 (768) → 19.7 (1024). Gold share 62.3% → 4.1%
  setup: GPT-2trunc on Wizard, gold forced in (an oracle setting, as the authors concede). At 128 tokens PPL is poor because some inputs contain only the context
  quote: "128 10.8 30.9 11.6 30.4 62.3%" ... "1024 10.7 19.7 11.3 19.4 4.1%"; "even if ground-truth is retained, once more noise is introduced, the performance of GPT-2trunc will become worse"
  where: p.12, Appendix C, Table 9

- claim: Letting the selector pick more sentences lowers perplexity but eventually lowers F1. Lower PPL is not the same as a better response.
  number: Wizard seen F1 22.0/21.3/21.1 and PPL 19.2/18.2/17.2 for Tmax=1/2/3. CMU_DoG F1 12.6/13.5/11.2
  setup: KnowledGPT, Table 6
  quote: "a larger Tmax also means more noise in generation. That is why when Tmax exceeds a value, F1 begins to drop."
  where: p.8–9, Table 6

- claim: The selector, trained without labels, beats a selector trained with labels (SKT) on selection accuracy against the gold sentence.
  number: 28.0 / 25.4 vs SKT 26.8 / 18.3 (seen/unseen)
  setup: Wizard knowledge-selection accuracy
  quote: "the accuracy scores of knowledge selection for SKT are 26.8 and 18.3 on Test Seen and Test Unseen respectively, while the two numbers are 28.0 and 25.4 respectively for KnowledGPT"
  where: p.8

- claim: Without labels, earlier selectors collapse, according to the paper's account of Kim et al. 2020.
  number: 27% → 0.3%
  quote: "when human labels are removed, the accuracy of knowledge selection drops from 27% to 0.3%"
  where: p.5

- claim: In human evaluation fluency is similar across models. KnowledGPT leads on knowledge relevance.
  number: Knowledge relevance 1.71/1.68/1.50 (Wizard seen/unseen, CMU_DoG) vs GPT-2trunc 1.22/1.20/1.06 and DRD 1.26/1.18/1.07. Fluency 1.89 vs 1.86 (trunc). Kappa ≥0.6
  setup: 300 sampled examples per test set, 3 annotators, scale 0–2. On Wizard only the gold knowledge was shown to annotators
  quote: "KnowledGPT 1.89 1.67 1.71 0.70 1.88 1.60 1.68 0.73 1.83 1.65 1.50 0.77"; "All kappa values are no less than 0.6"
  where: p.8, Table 4; p.7 footnote 3

- claim: In the ablation, the pseudo-label warm-up matters most on Wizard.
  number: F1 seen 22.0 → 18.3 without pseudo; 20.4 without joint; 21.2 without curriculum; 21.3 without RL
  setup: Table 5
  quote: "-pseudo 22.3 18.3 0.857 0.436 0.662"
  where: p.8

- claim: The knowledge itself is needed. DialoGPT (345M), fine-tuned without knowledge, has lower PPL but lower F1.
  number: F1 17.9/16.8/12.3 vs 22.0/20.5/13.5
  quote: "DialoGPT 16.0 17.9 20.0 16.8 16.9 12.3"
  where: p.12, Table 8

- claim: A bigger generator (345M) lowers PPL but does not raise F1.
  number: F1 22.0 vs 22.0 seen
  quote: "KnowledGPT (345M) 16.1 22.0 17.9 20.6 18.1 13.4"
  where: p.12, Table 10

LIMITS: All models are 2020-scale: GPT-2 117M/345M with a 1024-token limit. Scoring is unigram F1 and embedding overlap against a single human reply. There is no hallucination or faithfulness metric. Selection is at sentence level within one retrieved document, and the paper does not study the retrieval step itself ("we assume that knowledge is retrieved from documents", p.2). Tmax is tiny (1–2 sentences), and the paper never compares against a modern cross-encoder reranker followed by top-k. The authors concede that the max-token experiment is an oracle ("in practice, one has no way to perfectly locate the ground-truth", p.12). Human eval on Wizard showed annotators only the gold knowledge. The pseudo-labels depend on responses overlapping the knowledge; the authors note that CMU_DoG workers "do not refer to the external knowledge as much" (p.8), and "about 35% of the conversation has a weak correlation with the document" (p.12). There are no significance tests for the human eval or the ablations, and no cost or latency figures. The PPL comparisons are muddied, since truncation gives lower PPL than selection. Position and order of the knowledge are not studied.

BUILDS ON: Dinan et al., 2019 (Wizard of Wikipedia, TMN); Zhou et al., 2018b (CMU_DoG); Kim et al., 2020 (SKT, sequential latent knowledge selection); Lian et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020 (DRD, low-resource, arXiv:2002.10348); Li et al., 2019 (ITDD); Radford et al., 2019 (GPT-2); Devlin et al., 2018 (BERT); Sutton et al., 2000 (policy gradient); Clark and Manning, 2016 (baseline for variance reduction); Zhang et al., 2019c (DialoGPT).

CODE: None in the paper. Algorithm 1 (p.6) is pseudo-code: warm up with MLE on the pseudo-labels, then each step does an RL update of the selector and a curriculum update of GPT-2 with p = p0·e^(−λm).

FIGURES: Figure 1, "Architecture of the proposed model.", p.4. It shows the BERT context-aware encoder feeding the sequential selector, which emits D′, then data mixing with the pseudo D̄ and the reward path into GPT-2. It explains the select-then-generate loop with generator feedback faster than prose does. Table 9 (p.12) would make a better small chart for the course: F1 against token budget with the gold sentence forced in.

FIT AND OVERLAP WITH NOTES:
- Best fit is 06-generation-for-rag.md, "Order and size of the context". Table 9 and Table 6 are direct evidence that more context hurts even with the gold sentence present, alongside FiD (more passages help a fusion-trained reader) and ELI5. The two results pull against each other: FiD's reader is trained to fuse, while this GPT-2 concatenates. That contrast is worth stating.
- 05-chunking-query-parsing-and-reranking.md, Reranking (line ~451): this paper supports the JPMorgan claim (Zhao et al., NAACL 2024, a different Zhao) that recall alone is the wrong target. It is a sharpens-type citation. Note that its selector is a learned cross-encoder-style selector, not an off-the-shelf reranker.
- 01-rag-pipeline.md, "Measure each stage" (line 377): this paper extends the Dinan gold-vs-predicted paragraph. It gives selection accuracy of 28.0/25.4 without labels, against Dinan's best of 25.5%. That is consistent with the note, because the gold-vs-predicted gap persists. Mind the setup: the note's 25.5% is Dinan's selector on seen topics, and KnowledGPT's 28.0 is a different model.
- Nothing in the notes is contradicted. Two cautions: the two "Zhao et al." citations will collide in prose, so name the venue and year. And PPL drops as context grows while F1 falls, so don't cite PPL as quality.

PROBLEMS: The extraction is clean. The table headers run together (e.g., "Test Seen Test UnseenPPL F1"), but the column order is recoverable. There were no embedded instructions. "495570 nm" in Table 12 is an extraction artifact (likely 495–570). The PDF does not state an arXiv id.
